row.basis: almsgiving and cleansing
row.note: Jesus answers concern with cleansing by telling his hearers to give alms and declaring all clean; this directly parallels the commentary's given share that purifies what remains.

row.basis: giving to poor; righteousness remains forever
row.note: Paul joins scattering gifts to the poor with righteousness remaining forever; it combines the commentary's paid crop-share with its falāḥ and bāqī permanence.

row.basis: seed, bread, harvest of righteousness
row.note: God supplies seed to the sower and bread for food, multiplies seed, and increases a harvest of righteousness; its gift context maps the commentary's blessed crop-growth to ethical fruit.

row.basis: firstfruits holy; whole batch holy
row.note: Paul's firstfruits analogy makes the whole dough holy from its consecrated portion; it gives a precise cultic counterpart to the commentary's share whose giving cleanses the remainder.

row.basis: almsgiving atones for sin
row.note: Sirach compares water quenching fire with almsgiving atoning for sin; it makes explicit the purificatory result assigned to tezekkā's charitable share.

row.basis: redeeming wrong by mercy to poor
row.note: Daniel's Aramaic counsel tells the king to break off sins through righteousness and wrongs through mercy to the poor; it joins relief of need to moral rescue like the commentary's gift and purification.

row.basis: seventh-year field; needy eat its remnant
row.note: The seventh-year field is left so needy people eat and animals take its remainder; it concretizes the commentary's harvested land as holding a claim beyond the owner's consumption.

row.basis: field corners and gleanings at harvest
row.note: At reaping, field corners and gleanings must remain; this is a direct legal form of the commentary's crop-right owed at harvest.

row.basis: forgotten sheaf for vulnerable people; blessing
row.note: A forgotten sheaf must remain for the alien, orphan, and widow so God blesses the work; it links surrendered harvest portion to blessing as the commentary links giving to purified productive remainder.

row.basis: annual tithe of field yield
row.note: Israel must tithe all seed-yield of the field year by year; its stated annual crop measure closely meets the commentary's output-and-allotted-share facet.

row.basis: third-year tithe of produce distributed
row.note: After completing the third-year tithe of produce, it is given to Levite, alien, orphan, and widow; its distribution specifies whom a crop due supports.

row.basis: firstfruits given; blessing on household
row.note: Firstfruits and offerings given to priests make blessing rest on the household; it combines output-share and blessing in the commentary's z-k-w agricultural sequence.

row.basis: honor God with first produce
row.note: Honoring the LORD from wealth and all first produce provides a concise biblical practice behind the commentary's payment from crop or wealth.

row.basis: barns filled and vats overflowing
row.note: The verse pictures filled barns and overflowing vats after firstfruits; it supplies abundance as the outcome of offered produce, rather than generic prosperity.

row.basis: full tithe; heavens opened for blessing
row.note: The full tithe is brought to the storehouse and God opens heaven to pour out blessing; it makes a fixed due share and divinely granted increase mutually explicit.

row.basis: firstfruits and tithes of produce
row.note: Tobit carries firstfruits and tithes of produce to Jerusalem; the narrative embodies the commentary's zakāt-like harvest obligation in pious practice.

row.basis: third tenth for those in need
row.note: Tobit's third tenth goes to people for whom he has a duty of care; it supplies the vulnerable-recipient side of the commentary's harvest share.

row.basis: firstfruits of winepress and threshing floor
row.note: The Didache directs firstfruits from winepress, threshing floor, cattle, and sheep to prophets; it carries the commentary's harvest-due motif into early Christian community order.

row.basis: firstfruits given to poor
row.note: If no prophet is present, the Didache directs firstfruits to the poor; it makes the crop share a relief obligation, not private purification alone.

row.ref: Basil of Caesarea, Homily 6 on Luke 12:18
row.basis: hoarded grain and the poor
row.note: Basil reads the rich man's larger barns as hoarding surplus that belongs with the needy; this Christian interpretation makes explicit the commentary's alternative between a harvest shared and one retained for self.

row.basis: larger barns for all grain and goods
row.note: The rich man demolishes barns to store all his grain and goods; against the commentary's harvest-day due, it stages productive output withheld for self.

row.basis: alms; unfailing heavenly treasure
row.note: Jesus commands almsgiving and calls the resulting heavenly treasury unfailing; it directly associates relinquished share with the commentary's better and more-lasting outcome.

row.basis: rain-soaked land; useful crop; blessing
row.note: Land that has drunk repeated rain produces a crop useful to its cultivators and receives God's blessing; it closely matches the commentary's worked, growing field rather than mere pasture.

row.basis: thorns and thistles; curse and burning
row.note: The contrasting land bears thorns and thistles and approaches curse and burning; it gives an ethical version of the commentary's same-ground contrast between productive cultivation and vegetation headed for ruin.

row.basis: digging, clearing, planting; expected fruit
row.note: The vineyard-owner digs, clears stones, plants, and expects good grapes; divine care of a cultivated plot renders concrete the commentary's agricultural sense assigned to Rabb.

row.basis: no pruning or hoeing; briers; no rain
row.note: The ruined vineyard will neither be pruned nor hoed, so briers arise and rain is withheld; it is the inverse of the commentary's ploughed, watered, yielding field.

row.basis: vineyard expected justice and righteousness
row.note: Isaiah identifies the LORD's vineyard with Israel and its expected fruit with justice and righteousness; it makes the commentary's agricultural success an explicitly moral outcome.

row.basis: LORD as vineyard keeper watering and guarding
row.note: The LORD calls himself the vineyard's keeper, watering it continually and guarding it night and day; this closely clarifies the commentary's farm-steward sense of Rabb.

row.basis: sow righteousness; reap loyal love; break fallow ground
row.note: Hosea commands sowing righteousness, reaping loyal love, and breaking fallow ground while seeking the LORD; agricultural labor becomes the ethical transformation that the commentary casts as purification and lasting success.

row.basis: rain waters earth; sprouting; seed and bread
row.note: Rain and snow water the earth, make it sprout, and provide seed and bread; this gives a precise biblical water-to-growth-to-food field scene beside the commentary's expanded field imagery.

row.basis: rain in season; land produce and tree fruit
row.note: God's timely rain makes land yield produce and trees fruit; it places the commentary's crop growth under divine blessing.

row.basis: blade, head, full grain
row.note: Jesus's seed parable narrates the ordered growth of blade, head, and full grain; it gives a kingdom reading of the commentary's field-process.

row.basis: ripe grain; sickle; harvest
row.note: When the grain permits, the sickle is sent because harvest has arrived; it supplies the harvest-stage after the commentary's growth and cultivation.

row.basis: good soil bears fruit with endurance
row.note: Good soil is an honest, good heart that holds the word and bears fruit with endurance; it joins the commentary's cultivated crop to falāḥ as lasting in good.

row.basis: worldly care and wealth choke fruit
row.note: Worldly care and wealth are thorns that choke the word and make it unfruitful; this concretely meets the commentary's contrast between a worldly field and a fruitful, enduring one.

row.basis: Father as vinedresser
row.note: Jesus calls the Father the vinedresser; this is a direct Christian agricultural analogue for the commentary's Rabb who maintains and restores a farm.

row.basis: pruning cleans fruitful branches for more fruit
row.note: The vinedresser removes barren branches and prunes fruit-bearing ones so they bear more; it puts cleansing and maintenance directly inside a growth-to-fruit process.

row.basis: unabiding branch withers and is burned
row.note: A branch that does not remain withers and is gathered for fire; it supplies a pointed vegetal reverse to the commentary's crop that remains in good rather than becoming ruined growth.

row.basis: sowing to flesh or Spirit; corruption or eternal life
row.note: The two sowings culminate in corruption or eternal life; it gives direct field language to the commentary's contrast between a worldly crop and an afterlife-directed one.

row.basis: do good; reap in due season; do not give up
row.note: Doing good is to continue because one will reap in due season without giving up; it closely supplies the commentary's success as remaining in good.

row.basis: harvested fruit for eternal life
row.note: The reaper gathers fruit for eternal life, so sower and reaper rejoice together; it makes harvest an image of the enduring good emphasized at 87:17.

row.basis: farmer waits for precious fruit and rains
row.note: The farmer waits patiently for the earth's precious fruit and its rains while believers await the Lord; this connects crop maturation to the commentary's enduring, eschatological good.

row.basis: fruitful tree; leaf does not wither; prospers
row.note: The righteous person is a watered tree yielding fruit whose leaf does not wither and whose work prospers; it is a close vegetal counterpart to cultivated success and permanence.

row.basis: watered tree does not cease bearing fruit
row.note: The tree by water stays green through heat and drought and does not cease producing fruit; it directly contrasts durable blessed growth with the commentary's perishing pasture.

row.basis: break fallow ground; do not sow among thorns
row.note: Jeremiah's call to break fallow ground and avoid sowing among thorns applies ploughing to repentance; it strengthens the commentary's ethical reading of broken soil and fruitful cultivation.

row.basis: God teaches the farmer right practice
row.note: In Isaiah's farming instruction, the farmer's God teaches him the right practice; it offers an indirect biblical counterpart to the commentary's Lord who tends and orders a farm.

row.basis: seed dies in order to live
row.note: The commentary uses a seed smothered under soil as purification's opposite, whereas Paul makes a sown seed's death the necessary image of resurrection; the opposed agricultural valuation is the link.

row.basis: earth's ripe harvest and final reaping
row.note: The angel announces that the earth's harvest is ripe and must be reaped; it supplies an explicitly final-harvest horizon for the commentary's crop and afterlife contrast.

row.basis: Arabic ف ل ح; Hebrew פלח; cleaving ground
row.note: The commentary's Arabic ف ل ح is developed as splitting and ploughing soil; Hebrew פֹּלֵחַ depicts cleaving the ground in the psalm's simile, retaining the same concrete root-scene in a different setting.

row.basis: pe'ah as an unfixed harvest obligation
row.note: The Mishnah lists pe'ah, the field-edge left from harvest, among obligations with no fixed measure; this legal reception sharpens the commentary's claim that produce bears a due share.

row.basis: charity saving from Gehenna
row.note: Rabbi Akiva's defense of supporting the poor makes charity a means by which the giver is saved from Gehenna; it develops the commentary's charitable purification into a salvation claim.

row.basis: deeds as roots that withstand the wind
row.note: Avot compares deeds exceeding wisdom to a deeply rooted tree that wind cannot uproot; its moral agriculture gives a Jewish image for the commentary's remaining in good.

row.basis: vine and elm; rich support poor
row.note: Hermas makes the fruitful vine depend on the otherwise fruitless elm, then reads their mutual support as rich and poor aiding one another; it turns agricultural fruit into a specific charity relation.

row.basis: hardworking farmer's first share of crops
row.note: The hard-working farmer ought first to receive a share of the crops; this provides a distinct New Testament use of cultivation, labor, and a rightful portion beside the commentary's farmer and yield.

row.basis: Arabic ز ك و and Hebrew זכה; cleansing hands
row.note: If Hebrew זכה is accepted as cognate with the commentary's Arabic ز ك و label, Job's cleansing of the hands supplies a physical-purity use; the cognacy and semantic scope need verification.

row.basis: sowing six years and gathering field yield
row.note: Six years of sowing and gathering a field's yield supply the ordinary cultivated stage that the next verse interrupts for the needy; this completes the commentary's soil-to-yield process.

row.basis: vineyard gleanings left to poor and alien
row.note: Vineyard gleanings are explicitly left to the poor and resident alien; this supplies the recipient of the harvest-right developed in the commentary.

row.basis: protected land-fruit and nonfailing vine
row.note: After the tithe promise, God rebukes the devourer so it cannot destroy land-fruit or make the vine fail; it continues the commentary's due share with protected growth.

row.basis: hoarded goods fail to secure life
row.note: God demands the rich man's life that night and asks whose stored goods will be; it supplies the failed impermanence that turns the hoarded grain of Luke 12 into the commentary's worldly rather than lasting harvest.

row.basis: clean because of the spoken word
row.note: Within the vine and vinedresser discourse, Jesus calls the disciples clean because of his word; it gives a distinct purification claim beside the commentary's z-k-w cleansing within cultivated growth.

row.basis: ploughing and breaking the ground
row.note: Isaiah asks whether a ploughman keeps opening and breaking his ground all day; it names the physical soil-splitting scene beneath the commentary's Arabic falāḥ.

row.basis: leveled soil and ordered sowing
row.note: After leveling the soil, the farmer sows differentiated seed in appointed places; it supplies the ordered planting stage after the commentary's split earth.

row.basis: planting, watering, and God's growth
row.note: Paul plants, Apollos waters, but God gives the growth; this is an unusually exact divine growth sequence for the commentary's cultivated crop.

row.basis: God alone gives growth
row.note: Neither planter nor waterer is decisive, but God who gives growth; it identifies divine agency in the increase the commentary connects with blessing.

row.basis: God's cultivated field
row.note: Paul calls the community God's field; it converts the commentary's cared-for farm into a communal ethical image.

row.basis: fruit due from vineyard tenants
row.note: When fruit season approaches, the vineyard owner sends servants to receive the fruit due him; it is a direct narrative counterpart to the commentary's harvest carrying a rightful claim.

row.basis: kingdom given to fruit-producing people
row.note: The kingdom is given to people producing its fruits; the vineyard's fruit-duty becomes a moral criterion, like the commentary's link of field yield with successful purification.

row.basis: digging and fertilizing a fruitless tree
row.note: The vinedresser proposes digging around a fruitless fig tree and applying manure; it gives a close farm-repair image for the commentary's Rabb who tends and restores a plot.

row.basis: fruit or cutting after cultivation
row.note: Fruit in the coming year prevents cutting, while continued barrenness ends the tree; it makes growth versus ruin the condition of the cultivated plant.

row.basis: perishing food and food enduring to eternal life
row.note: Jesus contrasts food that perishes with food enduring to eternal life; it maps the commentary's food-and-field imagery onto its world-life and lasting-afterlife contrast.

row.basis: grass of the field is transient
row.note: Grass alive in the field today is thrown into an oven tomorrow; it gives a direct Gospel reverse to the commentary's durable good over perishing pasture.

row.basis: wheat gathered and weeds destroyed at harvest
row.note: At harvest the weeds are gathered for burning and the wheat stored in the barn; the same field distinguishes productive crop from destructive vegetation.

row.basis: grass dries and its flower falls
row.note: All flesh is grass whose flower falls when the grass dries; the formula closely matches the commentary's passing pasture image.

row.basis: word remains forever
row.note: The Lord's word remains forever after the grass-and-flower contrast; it supplies an explicit enduring term beside the commentary's abqā.

row.basis: perennial fruit and healing leaves
row.note: The tree of life bears fruit every month and its leaves heal nations; watered, recurring produce gives an eschatological image of durable blessed yield.

row.basis: earth sprouts seed-bearing plants and fruit trees
row.note: God commands the earth to sprout seed-bearing vegetation and fruit trees; it gives a creation-level counterpart to the commentary's God-brought pasture and growing crop.

row.basis: seedtime and harvest do not cease
row.note: Seedtime and harvest will not cease while the earth remains; this directly supplies a crop-cycle formulation for the permanence sought in the commentary.

row.basis: sowing, hundredfold yield, and divine blessing
row.note: Isaac sows the land, finds a hundredfold that year, and is blessed by the LORD; it closely combines cultivation, increase, and divine blessing.

row.basis: fourth-year fruit consecrated to God
row.note: All fruit of a newly planted tree's fourth year is holy praise for the LORD; it gives a concrete sacred setting-aside of harvest before later enjoyment.

row.basis: fifth-year eating so yield increases
row.note: In the fifth year people may eat the fruit so that the tree's yield increases; it explicitly joins a prior consecrated portion with continuing growth.

row.basis: barley firstfruits given for the people
row.note: A man brings barley firstfruits to the man of God, who orders that the people receive them to eat; it is a narrative enactment of harvest share becoming communal provision.

row.basis: all eat and some remains
row.note: After the shared firstfruits are set before the people, all eat and some remains by the LORD's word; it gives a concrete counterpart to the commentary's baqī as what is left from yield.

row.basis: eating land-yield without payment
row.note: Job denies eating his land's yield without payment or causing its owners to suffer; it makes a field's produce ethically answerable to those with a claim on it.

row.basis: thorns instead of wheat for unjust use
row.note: For such unjust use of land, Job accepts thorns instead of wheat and weeds instead of barley; it gives a juridical reverse to the commentary's worked field that yields good.

row.basis: grass for cattle and plants for human cultivation
row.note: God makes grass grow for cattle and plants for human cultivation, bringing food from earth; it closely parallels the commentary's divine bringing-forth of pasture and crop.

row.basis: giving to poor and enduring righteousness
row.note: The righteous scatter gifts to the poor and their righteousness stands forever; it joins the commentary's charitable share to its enduring-good result in the Hebrew source behind 2 Corinthians 9.

row.basis: scattering increases; withholding due brings want
row.note: One person scatters and yet increases, while another withholds what is due and comes to want; this is a compact wisdom analogue to the commentary's share-and-growth logic.

row.basis: generosity and reciprocal watering
row.note: The generous person is enriched, and the one who waters is watered; it links giving, water, and renewed plenty beside the commentary's blessed agricultural increase.

row.basis: rain for seed, abundant bread, and broad pasture
row.note: God gives rain for seed, rich bread from land, and broad pasture for livestock; this closely fills out the commentary's rain, crop, food, and pasture sequence.

row.basis: wilderness becomes a fruitful field
row.note: With spirit poured from on high, wilderness becomes a fruitful field and the field a forest; it turns divine outpouring into the commentary's increase-and-growth imagery.

row.basis: justice in wilderness and righteousness in fruitful field
row.note: Justice dwells in wilderness and righteousness abides in the fruitful field; it makes the commentary's agricultural success explicitly ethical.

row.basis: righteousness produces lasting peace and security
row.note: The work of righteousness yields peace, quietness, and security forever; it supplies the durable-good outcome to the fruitful-field image just developed.

row.basis: grass withers, but God's word stands forever
row.note: Grass withers and flowers fade, but God's word stands forever; it directly pairs the commentary's dying pasture with an enduring reality.

row.basis: earth and garden sprout righteousness
row.note: As earth brings sprouts and a garden causes seed to spring up, the LORD causes righteousness and praise to spring forth; this exactly translates crop growth into moral flourishing.

row.basis: grain, wine, oil, watered garden, never languishing
row.note: Restored people receive grain, wine, oil, and become like a watered garden that never languishes; it joins harvested goods to enduring blessed vitality.

row.basis: multiplied fruit trees and field produce
row.note: God promises to multiply fruit of trees and produce of fields so Israel no longer bears famine's reproach; it provides a restoration form of the commentary's blessed increase.

row.basis: fruit trees fed by holy water
row.note: Trees beside the life-giving water bear fruit monthly and healing leaves; their unfailing yield provides a vivid scriptural image of lasting, beneficial produce.

row.basis: prosperous seed, vine fruit, ground produce, dew
row.note: The promised seed prospers as vine yields fruit, ground gives produce, and heaven dew; it is a compact restoration sequence of growth and divine blessing.

row.basis: full threshing floors and overflowing vats
row.note: Threshing floors fill with grain and vats overflow with wine and oil; it gives a concrete harvest-abundance scene beside the commentary's output and yield.

row.basis: almsgiving delivers from death and purges sin
row.note: Tobit says almsgiving delivers from death and purges every sin; it is an exceptionally close Jewish formulation of the commentary's gift, purification, and salvation sequence.

row.basis: almsgiving rescues from death and darkness
row.note: Tobit's instruction says almsgiving delivers from death and keeps one from darkness; it supplies a second narrative exhortation linking charitable giving to lasting rescue.

row.basis: tithe so that one may become rich
row.note: The rabbinic reading of the tithe command derives, "tithe so that you may become rich"; it explicitly interprets a crop share as the path to increase, sharpening the commentary's z-k-w sequence.

row.basis: working and keeping the garden
row.note: God places the human in Eden to work and keep the garden; the human stewardship role is an indirect counterpart to the commentary's farm-maintaining Rabb.

row.basis: one-fifth harvest share and four parts retained
row.note: Joseph's harvest rule gives one fifth to Pharaoh and retains four parts for seed and food; in a fiscal rather than charitable setting, it closely mirrors the commentary's measured output-share and remainder.

row.basis: planters enjoy their own crop for enduring days
row.note: God's restored people will not plant for another to eat, but enjoy their work for days like a tree; it offers a secondary vision of rightful yield and durable enjoyment.

row.basis: a planted vine withers under the east wind
row.note: Though planted, the vine withers when struck by the east wind in its growing bed; it supplies a prophetic counterpart to the commentary's warning that a field can lose its crop.

row.basis: sowing without reaping under judgment
row.note: The judged people sow but do not reap, tread olives without oil, and grapes without wine; it reverses the commentary's expected process from cultivation to usable yield.

row.basis: sowing much but harvesting little
row.note: Haggai's audience sows much but brings in little and finds no satisfaction; it gives an economic and moral version of crop growth failing to become lasting good.

row.basis: gathering leftovers so nothing is lost
row.note: After all have eaten, Jesus orders the remaining fragments gathered so nothing is lost; this is a secondary food analogue for the commentary's baqī, the yield that remains.

row.basis: vineyard planter eats its fruit
row.note: Paul asks who plants a vineyard without eating its fruit; it offers a distinct New Testament use of farm labor and a rightful portion beside the commentary's farmer and yield.

row.basis: fruit of righteousness sown in peace
row.note: A fruit of righteousness is sown in peace by those who make peace; it gives a concise ethical sowing-and-yield image for the commentary's field of purified good.

row.basis: training yields peaceful fruit of righteousness
row.note: Discipline is painful at first but later yields peaceful fruit of righteousness to those trained; it gives a secondary purification-to-fruit sequence.

row.basis: generosity and readiness to share
row.note: The wealthy are commanded to be generous and ready to share; it directly develops the commentary's wealth-share aspect outside the harvest image.

row.basis: foundation for the future and true life
row.note: The result is a stored foundation for the future and grasping true life; it supplies a durable-life outcome for the generosity enjoined in the preceding verse.

row.basis: produce growing from earth liable to tithe
row.note: The Mishnah defines tithe-liable produce as food that is guarded and grows from the earth; this legal reception marks the crop-to-due boundary assumed by the commentary.
